subject: Agriculture
title: The Dust Bowl Locust Plagues
description: A 60-second lesson on The Dust Bowl Locust Plagues.

hook.text: In the 1870s, Rocky Mountain locusts formed swarms covering 510,000 km²—larger than California. Then they went extinct.

buildup.text: The swarm of 1875 contained an estimated 12.5 trillion insects—the largest animal aggregation ever recorded.

discovery.text: Locusts ate everything—crops, leather harnesses, wooden fence posts, and the clothes off people's backs.

twist.text: By 1902, the Rocky Mountain locust was extinct. Farmers had plowed up its breeding habitat in river valleys.

climax.text: The extinction was accidental—no one planned it. Habitat destruction solved a pest problem no one could otherwise stop.

punchline.text: Humanity's worst locust plague was accidentally eliminated by farming itself.

quiz.question: Why did the Rocky Mountain locust go extinct?
options: Farmers unknowingly plowed up its breeding habitat in river valleys

details.summary: The Dust Bowl era of the 1930s saw devastating grasshopper and locust plagues sweep across the American Great Plains, compounding the misery of drought and soil erosion. This topic covers how the plagues were linked to ecological disruption and the emergence of government pest control programs.
details.whyItMatters: The Dust Bowl locust plagues illustrate how land degradation and drought can trigger pest outbreaks. They led to the creation of federal pest control infrastructure that laid the groundwork for modern agricultural extension services.
takeaways: Grasshopper swarms in the 1930s destroyed crops already weakened by drought and erosion
Land degradation removed natural predator habitat, enabling pest population explosions
Federal response programs became the foundation of U.S. agricultural pest management

faq.question: Why did locust and grasshopper plagues intensify during the Dust Bowl?
faq.answer: Plowing up native grasslands destroyed habitat for grasshopper predators like birds and ground beetles. Drought stressed crops made them more vulnerable. Bare, warm soil provided ideal egg-laying conditions and hot, dry weather accelerated grasshopper development and swarming.

faq.question: How did the U.S. government respond to the Dust Bowl pest crisis?
faq.answer: The federal government launched emergency poisoned bait programs and hired unemployed workers to spread arsenic-bran mixtures. These efforts evolved into the USDA's ongoing grasshopper management program and demonstrated the need for organized, government-funded pest control infrastructure.
